To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there was no overall increase in the mean maternal weight from one pregnancy in England to the next; (2) 14.8 per cent of women gained more than 5 lb (2.27 kg) in association with their pregnancy; (3) women who had a higher BMI at the beginning of the pregnancy gained more weight from one successful pregnancy to the next; and (4) women who gained more weight in pregnancy and gave birth to heavier infants gained more weight from pregnancy

the average primiparous mother from England gains no more than 1 kg in weight from the start of her first pregnancy to the start of her second, but that 14.8 per cent of them gain more than 1 kg, with the risk factors being a high prepregnant BMI and a tendency to gain more weight during the first pregnancy.

the long-term weight change of women who have had a baby, and who may be at risk of obesity, and who may also be at increased risk of complications of pregnancy and adverse outcomes of the baby.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of pregnancy on long term weight gain of mothers in England is small and not statistically significant.
, for most women, pregnancy is not associated with an increase in long-term body weight.
, while most primiparous women do not gain weight during pregnancy, a small proportion do, and that this weight gain persists into the next pregnancy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pregnancy has little effect on the long-term change in body weight of most women, but may have a permanent effect on the weight of a small number.
pregnancy has a small but significant effect on the long-term body weight of primiparous English women, with the effect being greatest in mothers who were already obese at the beginning of pregnancy.
the impact of pregnancy is not as important as other factors in determining the weight gain of primiparae.
The main takeaway from our work is that

pregnancy is not a time of weight gain for most mothers, but rather a time of stability, and it should not be used to justify the development of policies aimed at increasing maternal weight gain during pregnancy.
, in order to reduce the incidence of maternal obesity, it is necessary to focus on the prepregnant period, and to identify women at risk of gaining excessive weight during pregnancy.
